name: Ryze
tagline: An AI assistant that collects your tasks, notes and calendar noise and hands back a plan for the day.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core of an AI planning assistant is a text box, a database table and one well written system prompt, and an agent will give you that in an afternoon. What it will not give you is the part that makes these apps work: a mobile app that is actually open when the thought arrives, push notifications that land at the right moment, and calendar OAuth that survives a token refresh. A local web app that you have to go visit will get used for nine days and then forgotten, which is the usual fate of self-built productivity tooling. If you live in a browser tab all day and want full control over the prompt and the data, the DIY version is genuinely fine. If the value for you is the nudge rather than the plan, buy it.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you dump unstructured notes and tasks, and an LLM returns a prioritised, time-blocked plan for the day that you can accept, edit and check off.
requirements: An LLM API key (OpenAI or Anthropic), billed per use
Node 20+ and a machine to run it on
Optional: a Google Cloud project if you want real calendar read access
whatYouLose: A mobile app, which is where capture actually happens
Push notifications and time-aware nudges instead of a tab you forgot to open
Calendar and task integrations that keep working after the first token expiry
Prompt tuning done by people who watched thousands of users ignore their suggestions
Sync across devices, and anything resembling a backup story
moatNotes: Assistants in this space compete on feel, timing and how little friction capture has, not on model access. Everyone has the same model.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of a planning assistant is not generating the plan, it is being present at the moment you need to offload something and then interrupting you later with exactly the right nudge. That means a phone app, background scheduling, notification permissions, and connectors to whatever calendar and task system you already use. A self-hosted web page does the reasoning just as well and the behaviour change not at all, and behaviour change is the whole product.
notes: Pricing and exact feature set here are unverified, treat the entry as a shape rather than a spec.
prompt:
Build a local-first AI day planner called Dayplan. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Next.js 14 App Router with TypeScript and Tailwind, run with `npm run dev`
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/dayplan.db, schema created on first boot
- Anthropic or OpenAI SDK, key read from .env.local as LLM_API_KEY, never hardcoded
- No auth, this binds to localhost only

Data model:
- items: id, text, status (inbox | planned | done | dropped), created_at, done_at, energy (low | high | null), est_minutes
- plans: id, date, generated_at, raw_json
- blocks: id, plan_id, item_id, start_time, end_time, rationale

Features that are in:
1. A single capture box on the home page. Type anything, hit enter, it lands in inbox as one item. Multi line paste splits into multiple items.
2. A "Plan my day" button. It sends all inbox and planned items plus the current time and a user supplied list of fixed commitments to the LLM, which returns strict JSON: ordered time blocks with start, end, item_id and a one sentence rationale. Validate the JSON with zod and retry once on failure.
3. A today view showing the blocks as a vertical timeline, each with a checkbox. Checking a block marks the item done.
4. Inline edit: drag to reorder blocks, delete a block, or drop an item back to inbox. Persist on every change.
5. A /review page: items completed per day for the last 14 days, and a list of items that have been re-planned three or more times, labelled honestly as "you are not going to do these".
6. The system prompt lives in prompts/planner.md as plain markdown so it can be edited without touching code.

Explicitly out of scope: mobile app, push notifications, calendar OAuth, sync, sharing, any hosted deployment.

Include a seed script with about 20 fake inbox items so the planner can be tested without typing, and a README with setup in under ten lines.
